title: Promises, async/await, and the event loop interview drills

items.question: Predict the output: console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);
items.answer: 1, 4, 3, 2. Synchronous 1 and 4 run first. The call stack empties. All microtasks drain — Promise.then logs 3. Then one macrotask runs — setTimeout logs 2. This is the core event-loop ordering puzzle.
followUps: Where does async/await fit in this ordering?
How is this different from C# Task continuations?
items.sixtySeconds: Sync first. Microtasks drain completely. Then one macrotask. Promise.then is microtask. setTimeout is macrotask.

items.question: Implement a minimal Promise with then and microtask scheduling.
items.answer: State: pending, fulfilled, rejected. resolve/reject once. Store handlers array. then returns new Promise. On settle, queueMicrotask to run handlers. Handler return adopts child Promise. Throw rejects child. Must not call handlers synchronously.
items.sixtySeconds: State machine. Subscribers. queueMicrotask. then returns new Promise. resolve once. promisify pattern for callbacks.

items.question: When do you use Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled in production?
items.answer: Promise.all when every result is required and one failure should fail the whole operation — dashboard loading profile, permissions, and notifications together. allSettled when partial success is acceptable — bulk health checks across microservices where you report which failed. all rejects fail-fast; allSettled never rejects the wrapper.
followUps: What happens to in-flight requests when all rejects?
How do you add a timeout?
items.sixtySeconds: all equals fail-fast parallel wait. allSettled for degraded mode. race for timeout with AbortSignal on loser.

items.question: Your Node service does await Promise.all(tenThousandIds.map(id => fetch(...))). What breaks?
items.answer: Unbounded concurrency opens thousands of sockets — EMFILE, upstream 429 rate limits, memory pressure. Fix with mapPool or semaphore capping in-flight work to 10–50. Still single-threaded JS but limits parallel I/O. Pair with AbortSignal on process shutdown.
followUps: Does the pool use multiple threads?
items.sixtySeconds: Promise.all unbounded. mapPool N workers shared index. Not multithreaded. SemaphoreSlim in C#. Abort on shutdown.

items.question: A candidate says Task is just a JavaScript Promise. Respond.
items.answer: Same programmer model — await, compose, cancel — different scheduler. JS Promise continuations are microtasks on one thread. C# Task continuations run on thread-pool threads and may hop threads. Promise.all maps to Task.WhenAll for concurrent waits, not CPU parallelism. JS has no ValueTask. AbortController is the practical CancellationToken analog.
followUps: Why is DOM access safe after await in JS?
items.sixtySeconds: Same syntax different engine. Microtasks one thread. Pool threads in C#. WhenAll equals all. AbortSignal equals token.

items.question: How do you cancel an in-flight fetch when the user types the next search character?
items.answer: AbortController per search: abort previous controller before starting new fetch. Pass signal to fetch. Catch AbortError and ignore — expected race. Debounce input to reduce calls. Do not rely on Promise.race alone without aborting the losing fetch.
followUps: Does abort free the socket immediately?
How does this compare to CancellationToken?
items.sixtySeconds: New AbortController per request. abort previous. signal on fetch. Ignore AbortError. Debounce keystrokes.

items.question: Explain async/await desugaring to Promises and microtasks.
items.answer: async function wraps return value in Promise. await expr means wait for Promise.resolve(expr) and resume via microtask when settled. Code after await in the same function runs as microtask callback, not macrotask. Errors become rejected Promise caught by try/catch around await.
followUps: What about await in a .then callback?
items.sixtySeconds: async returns Promise. await schedules microtask continuation. Not a macrotask. try/catch catches reject.

items.question: Load session from Redis cache or OAuth introspect endpoint concurrently — sketch the code.
items.answer: const [redisData, intro] = await Promise.all([redis.get(sessionId), fetch(introspectUrl, { signal }).then(r => r.text())]); return redisData ?? intro; Mirrors Task.WhenAll in C#. Shared AbortSignal cancels both on timeout. Neither parallelizes CPU — overlaps I/O waits on one thread.
followUps: When would you sequential await instead?
items.sixtySeconds: Promise.all for parallel I/O. Shared AbortSignal. WhenAll in C#. Sequential if second depends on first.
